text.title: Hot Path Baseline Template Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules fixing what a pre-optimisation baseline must capture: percentile distribution rather than a mean, the sample count that makes p99 meaningful, offered load and error rate alongside latency, histogram bucket bounds, coordinated-omission control, per-operation resource counters, and the environment the numbers are only valid in.

rule.statement: The baseline MUST record p50, p95, p99 and max for each measured operation. A mean (or a mean with a standard deviation) as the only latency figure is rejected, and no "average response time" may appear as a before/after comparison term.

rationale.source: Gil Tene — How NOT to Measure Latency

rule.rationale: Service latency is right-skewed and usually multi-modal — cache hit, cache miss, retry. The mean falls in the empty gap between modes, so it describes no request that actually happened, and one 30-second outlier moves it as much as thousands of fast requests. A change that halves the mean while doubling p99 is a regression that the mean reports as a win.

rule.statement: Every percentile MUST be published with its sample count `n` and the wall-clock measurement window. p99 requires n >= 1000 in the window; below that, record p50/p95 only and mark p99 as `insufficient-samples`. p99.9 requires n >= 10000.

rationale.source: Order-statistic sampling — a q-quantile needs ~1/(1-q) samples per observation above it

rule.rationale: At n = 100 the p99 estimate is a single observation, so it is the max under a different name and it swings by an order of magnitude between runs. A refactor "improving p99 by 40%" measured over 100 requests is measuring run-to-run noise.

rule.statement: Latency figures MUST be accompanied by the offered load (requests/sec or concurrency level) and the error rate over the same window — the RED triple: Rate, Errors, Duration. A latency number with no stated load is rejected, and any window whose error rate exceeds 1% is rejected as a baseline.

rationale.source: RED method (Tom Wilkie); USE method (Brendan Gregg)

rule.rationale: Latency is a function of utilisation, and it rises non-linearly near saturation, so p99 at 10 rps and p99 at 900 rps are unrelated numbers. Errors invalidate the window independently: failed requests usually return fast, so a burst of 500s pulls every percentile down and can be reported as an improvement.

rule.statement: When percentiles come from a bucketed histogram (Prometheus `histogram_quantile`, OpenTelemetry explicit-bucket histograms), the artefact MUST record the bucket boundaries and note whether the target percentile fell in the top finite bucket. Percentiles from separate shards or time windows MUST be recomputed from merged histograms, never averaged.

rationale.source: Prometheus histogram_quantile docs; HdrHistogram / t-digest merge semantics

rule.rationale: `histogram_quantile` interpolates linearly inside the bucket the quantile lands in, so if the highest finite bucket is 1s and true p99 is 4s, the reported value is pinned near 1s and never moves however bad latency gets. Averaging percentiles is invalid for the separate reason that quantiles are not additive — the mean of two shards' p99 is not the p99 of the union.

rule.statement: The artefact MUST name the load generator and its scheduling mode, and that mode MUST be open-loop / constant-arrival-rate — k6 `constant-arrival-rate`, Gatling `constantUsersPerSec`, `wrk2` with `-R`, or JMeter with a precise throughput timer. Closed-loop tools that issue the next request only after the previous response (`ab`, default `wrk`, a naive loop) are recorded as `coordinated-omission-uncorrected` and their high percentiles are marked unusable.

rationale.source: Gil Tene — coordinated omission; HdrHistogram recordValueWithExpectedInterval

rule.rationale: A closed-loop client stops sending while the system is stalled, so the requests that would have landed inside a 2-second pause are never issued and never timed. The stall is recorded as one slow sample instead of thousands, which can understate p99 by more than an order of magnitude — exactly the regime the baseline exists to detect.

rule.statement: Beyond latency the baseline MUST capture, per operation: bytes allocated and allocation count (Go `go test -benchmem` → `B/op`, `allocs/op`; JVM allocation rate via JFR), cache hit ratio with eviction count (Redis `INFO stats` → `keyspace_hits`, `keyspace_misses`, `evicted_keys`), and dependency fan-out — SQL query count and outbound HTTP call count per request.

rationale.source: Go testing -benchmem; Redis INFO stats; N+1 query pattern

rule.rationale: Latency alone cannot attribute a regression. Allocation counts expose GC pressure that appears only under sustained load rather than in a single-request trace; the fan-out counter is what distinguishes an N+1 from a genuinely slow query, and a cache "hit ratio" recorded without eviction count hides a cache that is thrashing at its memory ceiling and will collapse as data grows.

rule.statement: The artefact MUST pin the environment the numbers are valid in: commit SHA, build flags/optimisation level, runtime version, instance type or CPU model, and dataset size or row count. The after-measurement MUST reuse every one of these values; if any differs, the comparison is labelled `not-comparable` rather than reported as a delta.
rule.rationale: Latency on shared cloud instances varies with CPU steal, frequency scaling and neighbour load by more than most optimisations gain, and query latency tracks table size, so a baseline taken on last month's smaller dataset makes any later measurement look like a regression. Without the pinned tuple there is no way to tell an optimisation from a change of machine.
